title: Twilight Zone
description: Correction. The Ventures' track is called "Twilight Zone" and closes side two of their 1964 Dolton LP The Ventures in Space. The album's credits give it to Marty Manning, which means it is the tune from Manning's 1961 Columbia LP The Twilight Zone, not Marius Constant's TV theme. The same album opens with "Out of Limits", the Marketts' near-copy of the Constant motif.
tz_connection: A space-themed surf-instrumental take on Marty Manning's Twilight Zone-inspired piece, on the same LP as "Out of Limits".
recommendation_reason: A well-known 1964 surf-rock entry. The writer credit corrects the assumption that this is the TV theme.

title: The Twilight Zone Tower of Terror – attraction music
description: The music of the attraction comes in three layers. In the lobby and queue, 1930s-style jazz and period recordings set the hotel in 1939. Attractions Magazine names Duke Ellington's "Mood Indigo" and Vera Lynn's "We'll Meet Again" for the Paris version. In the library pre-show, Richard Bellis's score frames Serling's introduction. On the ride itself, the music and effects follow Herrmann's style. Paris got new ride audio for its 2007 and 2019 versions. Fan sites keep loop lists, but there has been no official album.
tz_connection: Licensed Twilight Zone music in the Disney attractions.
recommendation_reason: Connects the music category to the existing Tower of Terror ride records.

title: Herrmann's "Moat Farm Murder" cues in The Twilight Zone
creator: Bernard Herrmann
description: Bernard Herrmann scored "The Moat Farm Murder", a 1946 Mercury Summer Theatre broadcast starring Orson Welles, for CBS radio. The music went into the CBS stock library and was later cut into Twilight Zone episodes. Reba Wissner (Music, Sound and the Moving Image, 2017) traces the cues to eleven episodes and notes that Robert Drasnin compiled the stock scores for three of them.
tz_connection: Herrmann's radio score was reused as stock music in eleven original-series episodes.
recommendation_reason: Shows how radio-era CBS music shaped the sound of the series. The academic source is public.
